title: PostgreSQL Index Fundamentals
description: Understand database index anatomy, access methods, trade-offs between read acceleration and write overhead.

data.text: An **index** is an auxiliary data structure on disk that enables the PostgreSQL query engine to locate target rows in `O(log N)` time instead of performing a sequential table scan (`O(N)`). While indexes dramatically speed up read queries, each index incurs write overhead on every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`.

rows: Default for scalar values, primary keys, foreign keys, timestamps
Multi-key objects: JSONB, text search (tsvector), arrays
Geometric points, PostGIS geometries, range types (TSTZRANGE)
Massive append-only time-series tables physically clustered by date
Exact equality lookups on long string keys (WAL-logged since PG 10)

data.text: Create an Index and Prove It Is Used

An index is only useful if the planner chooses it. Create the index, compare the plan before and after, and confirm that the plan changed from a sequential scan to an index scan. If it did not change, the query may not be sargable or the table may be too small for the planner to care.

data.title: Before and after an index
data.content: The plan before the index shows a Seq Scan; after the index the planner uses an Index Scan with a much lower row estimate cost.
data.code:
-- Before: sequential scan over every row
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
-- Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..1943.00 rows=3 width=64)
--   Filter: (customer_id = 42)

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

-- After: the index locates the matching rows directly
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id on orders
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
--   Buffers: shared hit=4

data.title: Interview angle: every index has a cost
data.text: An index speeds up reads but slows down every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on that table, and it consumes disk and cache. The right answer to 'should I add an index?' names the write path and the storage cost, not just the read benefit. Audit with `pg_stat_user_indexes` for indexes that are never used, and drop them — unused indexes are pure overhead.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: B-tree is the default index type in PostgreSQL.
Indexes trade read speed for write latency and disk storage.
Audit unused indexes using `pg_stat_user_indexes` to reclaim performance.
